coverage_criteria: Student can write the code to open a URL, load its content as a NumPy array, and slice the columns into features and labels.

current_subject_concepts.label: Text Summarization Objectives
current_subject_concepts.description: Text summarization aims to condense information from one or more source texts into a shorter version that preserves the main ideas and important content, serving as a tool for accessibility and efficient information retrieval.
coverage_criteria: Student can state the primary goal of text summarization and list its benefits for readers and producers.

current_subject_concepts.label: Mono-document vs Multi-document Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: Summarization can be classified by the number of input documents: mono-document summarization produces a summary from a single text, while multi-document summarization synthesizes information from multiple related documents, often dealing with greater information volume.
coverage_criteria: Student can differentiate between mono-document and multi-document summarization and provide an example scenario for each.

current_subject_concepts.label: Extractive vs Abstractive Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: Extractive summarization selects and concatenates unchanged sentences from the source text, while abstractive summarization may rephrase or generate new sentences, potentially altering structure and meaning, and requiring more complex NLP.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the difference between extractive and abstractive summarization, and identify which is more complex and why.

current_subject_concepts.label: Indicative vs Informative Summaries
current_subject_concepts.description: Indicative summaries provide a vague idea of the content and cannot replace the source, while informative summaries preserve the main content and can act as substitutes, allowing users to understand the subject without reading the full text.
coverage_criteria: Student can distinguish between indicative and informative summaries and explain when each is more appropriate.

current_subject_concepts.label: Generic vs User-Oriented Summaries
current_subject_concepts.description: Generic summaries present the most important information without considering the user's background, while user-oriented summaries tailor the content based on the user's knowledge, providing context for novices or novelty for experts.
coverage_criteria: Student can differentiate between generic and user-oriented summaries and describe a scenario where user-oriented would be beneficial.

current_subject_concepts.label: Supervised vs Unsupervised Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: Supervised summarization treats sentence inclusion as a classification task trained on labeled examples, while unsupervised summarization uses pre-defined features and heuristics to determine sentence importance without needing training data.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised approaches to summarization and give an example of each.

current_subject_concepts.label: Intermediate Representation in Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: The first step of summarization processing is creating an intermediate representation that captures the main aspects of the text, such as topic representations using word frequency tables or more complex indicators.
coverage_criteria: The student can define intermediate representation and describe one common method.

current_subject_concepts.label: Sentence Scoring for Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: After intermediate representation, each sentence receives a score indicating its importance, often based on how well it expresses key topics or a combination of indicator evidence, sometimes using machine learning.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain the purpose of sentence scoring and describe a common method.

current_subject_concepts.label: Sentence Selection Algorithms
current_subject_concepts.description: The summarization system selects a set of high-scoring sentences to form a summary, using greedy approaches that recalculate importance considering redundancy, or global optimization maximizing importance and coherence.
coverage_criteria: The student can describe the goal of sentence selection and outline one approach.

current_subject_concepts.label: Reformulation in Abstractive Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: In abstractive summarization, a final reformulation step rewrites or paraphrases the selected content to produce a fluent summary, often using natural language generation.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain when reformulation is applied and its role.

current_subject_concepts.label: Compression Rate in Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: Compression rate defines the size of the summary relative to the source text; e.g., a 60% compression rate means the summary will be 40% of the original length.
coverage_criteria: The student can define compression rate and calculate target summary length.

current_subject_concepts.label: Extractive Summarization Example with Python and NLTK
current_subject_concepts.description: An extractive summarization workflow in Python using urllib, BeautifulSoup, NLTK for tokenization and stopword removal, then scoring sentences by word frequency to select the top sentences.
coverage_criteria: The student can list the main steps: fetching data, parsing HTML, tokenizing, removing stopwords, creating frequency distribution, scoring sentences, and selecting top sentences.

current_subject_concepts.label: BERT Sentence Embeddings and K-Medoid Clustering for Extractive Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: Pre-trained BERT models convert sentences into fixed-length embeddings, which are then clustered using K-medoid to select representative sentences as the extractive summary, ensuring selected sentences are actual text excerpts.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain how BERT creates sentence embeddings and how K-medoid clustering selects sentences.
The student can contrast K-means and K-medoid for this task.

current_subject_concepts.label: Fine-tuning GPT-2 for Abstractive Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: GPT-2 is fine-tuned with a multi-loss strategy combining language modeling and multiple-choice prediction, using special tokens like <summarize> and keywords as input, with masked self-attention ensuring auto-regressive generation.
coverage_criteria: The student can describe the two training objectives (language modeling and multiple-choice) and their weighting.
The student can explain the role of special tokens and masked self-attention in the fine-tuning process.

current_subject_concepts.label: Keyword Extraction for Abstractive Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: In the abstractive summarization pipeline, important keywords (nouns and verbs) are automatically extracted using techniques like NLTK POS tagging or fine-tuned BERT, providing a condensed representation for the summarization model.
coverage_criteria: The student can name at least one method for keyword extraction and explain how keywords are used in the summarization input.

current_subject_concepts.label: Data Scarcity in Domain-Specific Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: Low availability of domain-specific data (e.g., only 35k pairs in COVID-19 research vs 286k in general datasets) and rare terminology can hinder effective fine-tuning of large models like BERT and GPT-2.
coverage_criteria: The student can quantify the data size challenge and explain why limited domain data degrades fine-tuning.

current_subject_concepts.label: Future Direction: Hybrid Extractive-Abstractive Summarization
current_subject_concepts.description: A suggested future approach is to feed sentences extracted by extractive summarization directly into an abstractive model, potentially improving summary quality by providing richer context.
coverage_criteria: The student can summarize this future work suggestion and discuss one potential benefit.

current_subject_concepts.label: Feature Extraction in NLP
current_subject_concepts.description: The process of transforming cleaned text into numerical features that machine learning algorithms can process, a fundamental step in NLP pipelines.
coverage_criteria: Explain why text needs to be converted to numbers for ML models.
List common feature extraction methods (e.g., BoW, TF-IDF, embeddings).
Describe the role of feature extraction in an NLP pipeline.

current_subject_concepts.label: Implementing Feature Extraction in Python for NLP
current_subject_concepts.description: Practical implementation of NLP feature extraction pipelines using Python libraries such as scikit-learn, NLTK, and spaCy, including loading text data and applying methods like CountVectorizer.
coverage_criteria: Can write code that loads text data and applies a feature extraction method (e.g., using scikit-learn's CountVectorizer).
Can describe common Python libraries used for NLP feature extraction.

current_subject_concepts.label: Building a Python Web API to Serve NLP Models
current_subject_concepts.description: Developing a Python-based web API to serve NLP models, using frameworks like Flask or FastAPI, including steps to wrap a model into a REST endpoint and considerations like latency and data serialization.
coverage_criteria: Can outline steps to wrap an NLP model into a simple REST API using Python.
Can identify challenges in serving NLP models via APIs (e.g., latency, data serialization).

current_subject_concepts.label: Creating a Basic Flask API Endpoint
current_subject_concepts.description: Setting up a minimal Flask application by importing Flask, creating an instance, defining a route with @app.route to bind a view function that returns data (e.g., JSON), and running the app. This forms the basis for a simple API endpoint.
coverage_criteria: Can write a minimal Flask app that defines a route returning a string or JSON.
Can explain how the @app.route decorator registers a URL endpoint.

current_subject_concepts.label: Handling Dynamic URL Parameters and URL Generation in Flask
current_subject_concepts.description: Using Flask's variable rules to capture dynamic parts of a URL (e.g., <int:user_id>) and employing url_for() to generate URLs for view functions, promoting maintainable and flexible endpoint design.
coverage_criteria: Can write a route with a dynamic path segment and enforce type with converters.
Can use url_for() to generate a URL to a given view function, including passing arguments.

current_subject_concepts.label: Defining API endpoints with HTTP methods in Flask
current_subject_concepts.description: Specify allowed HTTP methods with the methods argument to @app.route; use request.method to branch, or use shortcut decorators @app.get/@app.post.
coverage_criteria: Can create a route that handles both GET and POST
Can use request.method to distinguish request types
Can rewrite using separate @app.get and @app.post decorators

current_subject_concepts.label: NLP Vocabulary: Document, Body, Dictionary, Topic
current_subject_concepts.description: In NLP, a document is a single data instance (e.g., a paragraph, tweet). The body (or corpus) is the collection of all documents. The dictionary is the set of all unique words occurring in at least one document. A topic is a collection of co-occurring words that represent a theme.
coverage_criteria: Define the terms document, body (corpus), dictionary, and topic in NLP.

current_subject_concepts.label: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) Definition
current_subject_concepts.description: LSA is an unsupervised NLP technique that discovers latent topics in a corpus by applying dimensionality reduction (via SVD) to the document-term matrix, yielding lower-dimensional encodings of documents as combinations of topics.
coverage_criteria: Explain what LSA is and its purpose in text analysis.

current_subject_concepts.label: Document-Term Matrix in LSA
current_subject_concepts.description: A document-term matrix is a representation where rows correspond to documents, columns to dictionary words, and cells indicate word presence or frequency. It serves as the input to SVD in LSA.
coverage_criteria: Describe the structure of a document-term matrix.

current_subject_concepts.label: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in LSA
current_subject_concepts.description: In LSA, Singular Value Decomposition is applied to the document-term matrix to reduce its dimensionality and extract latent topics, analogous to PCA. This transforms the high-dimensional word space into a lower-dimensional topic space.
coverage_criteria: State the role of SVD in LSA and its analogy to PCA.

current_subject_concepts.label: String Encoding and Decoding in Python
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding that strings in Python 3 are sequences of Unicode characters, and how to encode strings to bytes using specified encodings (e.g., UTF-8) and decode bytes back to strings, handling potential encoding errors.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the difference between a string and a bytes object.
Given a string and an encoding name, student can write code to encode and decode it correctly.

current_subject_concepts.label: N-grams para Predição de Texto
current_subject_concepts.description: Define n-grams como sequências contíguas de n itens de um texto, usados em modelos de linguagem para prever a próxima palavra baseando-se em probabilidades.
coverage_criteria: Definir unigrama, bigrama e trigrama com exemplos.
Calcular a probabilidade de uma palavra dado o contexto do n-grama.

current_subject_concepts.label: Desafios do PLN: Ortografia, Neologismos e Figuras de Linguagem
current_subject_concepts.description: Cobre desafios relacionados a erros ortográficos, neologismos, figuras de linguagem e abreviações, que exigem tratamento especial em sistemas de PLN.
coverage_criteria: Explicar como erros ortográficos afetam o PLN.
Dar exemplos de neologismos e figuras de linguagem que são desafiadores.

current_subject_concepts.label: Desafios do PLN: Correferência, Negação e Recursos Limitados
current_subject_concepts.description: Discute desafios de correferência, negação e especulação, e a limitação de recursos para língua portuguesa, incluindo a WordNet.Br.
coverage_criteria: Explicar o que é correferência e dar um exemplo.
Descrever o desafio de identificar negação em textos médicos.
Citar um recurso de PLN para português.

current_subject_concepts.label: Ferramentas Google Cloud NLP
current_subject_concepts.description: Apresenta as ferramentas do Google Cloud para PLN: API Natural Language, AutoML Natural Language, Dialogflow e Document AI, explicando suas funções e diferenças.
coverage_criteria: Descrever o propósito da API Natural Language e do AutoML Natural Language.
Explicar a diferença entre Dialogflow e Document AI.

current_subject_concepts.label: scikit-learn: Visão Geral e Algoritmos de Classificação, Regressão e Clustering
current_subject_concepts.description: Apresenta a biblioteca scikit-learn para machine learning em Python, incluindo classificação, regressão, clustering, seleção de modelos e pré-processamento.
coverage_criteria: Identificar scikit-learn como biblioteca de ML.
Listar tarefas de ML suportadas (classificação, regressão, clustering).
Citar exemplos de algoritmos em cada categoria.

current_subject_concepts.label: NLP Definition
current_subject_concepts.description: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a subfield of AI that focuses on enabling computers to understand, process, and derive meaning from human language, leveraging linguistics and computer science, often relying on statistical approximations.
coverage_criteria: Define NLP as a subfield of AI that enables machines to read and understand human language.
Identify that NLP combines linguistics and computer science or relies on statistical methods.
Give an example of an NLP application (e.g., chatbots, sentiment analysis, information extraction).

current_subject_concepts.label: Everyday Applications of NLP
current_subject_concepts.description: Recognize and list common everyday applications of NLP, such as autocorrect and plagiarism checkers.
coverage_criteria: List and describe two everyday NLP applications, such as autocorrect and plagiarism checking.

current_subject_concepts.label: Broad NLP Applications with Explanation
current_subject_concepts.description: List a wide range of NLP applications and explain how NLP is used in at least one, demonstrating deeper understanding beyond mere recall.
coverage_criteria: Citar pelo menos cinco aplicações de PLN.
Escolher uma aplicação e explicar como o PLN é usado.

current_subject_concepts.label: NLP Challenges
current_subject_concepts.description: Natural Language Processing faces fundamental difficulties including text segmentation, ambiguity, context interpretation, semantic extraction, and the inherent variability of natural language where similar words can have different meanings and identical meanings can be expressed differently, making it distinct from processing structured data.
coverage_criteria: Explain the challenge of text segmentation with an example.
Describe how ambiguity can make interpretation difficult with an example.
Give an example where similar words convey different meanings and explain why NLP needs special approaches compared to tabular data.

current_subject_concepts.label: Text Preprocessing and Normalization
current_subject_concepts.description: The essential steps of cleaning and standardizing raw text for NLP, including lowercasing, removing punctuation, special characters, HTML tags, stop words, and tokenization, to reduce noise and ensure uniformity.
coverage_criteria: List the common text preprocessing steps and explain the purpose of each.
Apply preprocessing to a given raw text sample, including lowercasing, removing punctuation and stop words, and tokenization.

current_subject_concepts.label: Bag-of-Words Model Definition and Vocabulary Construction
current_subject_concepts.description: The bag-of-words (BOW) model represents documents as fixed-length vectors of word counts, using a vocabulary built from unique words across the corpus. Word order and grammar are disregarded, and documents are represented as vectors with each dimension corresponding to a vocabulary word.
coverage_criteria: Define the BOW model and explain how it converts text into word count vectors, disregarding word order and grammar.
Define vocabulary in BOW, explain how it determines vector dimensions, and how out-of-vocabulary words are handled.

current_subject_concepts.label: Bag of Words with scikit-learn's CountVectorizer
current_subject_concepts.description: Using CountVectorizer from scikit-learn to convert text documents into a term-document matrix of token counts. Students configure parameters such as max_features, n-gram range, and preprocessing options, then apply fit_transform to generate the matrix and interpret the output.
coverage_criteria: Instantiate CountVectorizer with parameters like max_features and fit_transform a list of texts to obtain a sparse matrix.
Explain how parameters (e.g., max_features) control vocabulary size and interpret the resulting term-document matrix.

current_subject_concepts.label: TF-IDF Definition and Computation
current_subject_concepts.description: TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) is a statistical measure used to evaluate the importance of a term to a document in a corpus. It is computed as the product of term frequency (TF), normalized by document length, and inverse document frequency (IDF), which scales down terms that appear in many documents. The resulting weight highlights terms that are frequent in a specific document but rare across the corpus.
coverage_criteria: Define TF-IDF and its components (TF and IDF), and explain its purpose in highlighting important words.
Compute TF, IDF, and TF-IDF for a given term in a small corpus.
Explain why TF-IDF improves over simple term frequency and identify when to use it in text analysis.

current_subject_concepts.label: TF-IDF concept and TfidfVectorizer weighting
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding how TF-IDF assigns weights based on term frequency and inverse document frequency, making discriminative terms more important than count-based Bag of Words.
coverage_criteria: Define TF-IDF and explain how it differs from simple count-based vectorization.

current_subject_concepts.label: Implementing TF-IDF with TfidfVectorizer in Python
current_subject_concepts.description: Using scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer to compute TF-IDF matrix from text, including preprocessing like stopword removal with NLTK.
coverage_criteria: Write code to import TfidfVectorizer, include stopwords from NLTK, and fit_transform a list of documents.

current_subject_concepts.label: One-Hot Encoding Definition
current_subject_concepts.description: One-hot encoding represents each word as a sparse vector with a 1 at the vocabulary index and zeros elsewhere, resulting in high-dimensional, inefficient representations.
coverage_criteria: Create a one-hot vector for a given word from a small vocabulary.
Explain why one-hot vectors are sparse and high-dimensional.

current_subject_concepts.label: One-Hot Encoding Implementation and Comparison
current_subject_concepts.description: One-hot encoding implementation and analysis, including producing one-hot vectors, explaining the dimensionality problem, and comparing one-hot encoding to dense embeddings.
coverage_criteria: Produce a one-hot vector for a word from a given vocabulary.
Explain the dimensionality problem with one-hot encoding for large vocabularies.
Compare one-hot encoding to dense embeddings.

current_subject_concepts.label: Multi-label Encoding with Binary Vectors
current_subject_concepts.description: In multi-label classification, labels are encoded as binary vectors where each index corresponds to a label, allowing a single example to have multiple 1s, unlike one-hot encoding for multi-class.
coverage_criteria: Encode a set of labels for a given text using a binary vector, and contrast with one-hot encoding for multi-class.

current_subject_concepts.label: Sigmoid Activation for Multi-label Classification
current_subject_concepts.description: For multi-label text classification with a bag-of-words model, the output layer should use sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy loss, as it allows independent binary predictions per label, while softmax is for multi-class.
coverage_criteria: Explain why sigmoid activation is preferred over softmax for multi-label classification, and select the appropriate loss function.

current_subject_concepts.label: Naive Bayes Classifier Core Concept
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding the Naive Bayes classifier as a probabilistic method that applies Bayes' theorem with naive independence assumption to compute class posterior probabilities, without performing explicit calculations.
coverage_criteria: State the naive independence assumption
Describe how Naive Bayes uses Bayes theorem for classification
Identify that it is an eager learning algorithm

current_subject_concepts.label: Naive Bayes Probability Calculation
current_subject_concepts.description: Applying Bayes' theorem with independence to compute class-conditional probabilities from term frequencies for text classification.
coverage_criteria: State Bayes theorem and apply to classification
Explain independence assumption and its effect on factoring P(X|y)
Calculate class probability from term frequencies

current_subject_concepts.label: Zero Frequency Error and Laplace Smoothing Concept
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding that zero frequency error occurs when a feature value is unseen in training, and that Laplace smoothing adds a small constant to counts to prevent zero probabilities, with the parameter α controlling the smoothing strength.
coverage_criteria: Define zero frequency error.
Explain how Laplace smoothing mitigates the error.
Describe the effect of the smoothing parameter α.

current_subject_concepts.label: Applying Laplace Smoothing in Naive Bayes
current_subject_concepts.description: Ability to apply Laplace smoothing to word count tables using the formula (count + 1) / (total words + vocabulary size) to avoid zero probabilities for unseen words.
coverage_criteria: Explain the zero probability problem.
Apply Laplace smoothing to word count tables.

current_subject_concepts.label: Distributional Hypothesis
current_subject_concepts.description: The distributional hypothesis states that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. It is the foundation for distributional semantics and word embeddings, allowing meaning to be inferred from contextual usage patterns.
coverage_criteria: State the distributional hypothesis.
Explain how the hypothesis justifies using word embeddings to represent meaning.
Given example sentences, identify words that are likely semantically related based on shared contexts.
Explain why antonyms like 'hot' and 'cold' can be considered similar under this hypothesis.

current_subject_concepts.label: Word Embeddings as Dense Vector Representations
current_subject_concepts.description: Words can be represented as dense, low-dimensional vectors in a continuous space, where semantically similar words have similar vectors, and vector dimensions capture latent semantic features. This contrasts with sparse representations like one-hot or bag-of-words.
coverage_criteria: Explain what word embeddings are and how they differ from sparse representations.
Give an example of semantic relationships captured by embeddings (e.g., analogies).
Describe how vector dimensions can represent features like authority or gender.

current_subject_concepts.label: Similarity Measures for Word Vectors: Cosine and Euclidean
current_subject_concepts.description: Canonical understanding of similarity measures for word vectors, including defining cosine similarity, explaining its preference over dot product, computing both cosine similarity and Euclidean distance, and understanding the differences and when to use each.
coverage_criteria: Define cosine similarity and explain why it is preferred over dot product for word vectors.
Compute cosine similarity between two given vectors.
Compute Euclidean distance between two given vectors.
Explain the differences between Euclidean distance and cosine similarity and identify scenarios where each is more appropriate.

current_subject_concepts.label: Word2Vec Architectures: CBOW and Skip-gram
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding the two primary Word2Vec architectures: Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) predicts a target word from context words, while Skip-gram predicts context words from a target word. Both produce dense word embeddings from unlabeled text.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate CBOW and Skip-gram, stating what each predicts and describing the input/output of each architecture.
Explain how Word2vec creates dense word vectors from unlabeled text.

current_subject_concepts.label: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation (Implementation)
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding how GloVe uses a co-occurrence matrix to generate word embeddings and contrasting with Word2Vec's local window approach, with an implementation focus.
coverage_criteria: Explain how GloVe uses a co-occurrence matrix to learn word embeddings.
Compare GloVe's approach to Word2Vec's context-window method.

current_subject_concepts.label: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation (Math)
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding the mathematical formulation of GloVe, where vectors are trained such that their dot product approximates the log of co-occurrence probability, incorporating global statistics.
coverage_criteria: Explain how GloVe differs from Word2vec regarding global information.
Describe the role of the co‑occurrence matrix in GloVe.

current_subject_concepts.label: Understanding Word2Vec Analogies
current_subject_concepts.description: Understanding that word2vec embeddings encode semantic relationships, enabling analogy solving through vector arithmetic.
coverage_criteria: Explain how word2vec vectors can be used to solve analogies.
Provide an example of analogy using vector operations.

current_subject_concepts.label: Applying Vector Arithmetic for Analogies
current_subject_concepts.description: Performing vector arithmetic (addition/subtraction) with word2vec embeddings to solve semantic analogy tasks.
coverage_criteria: Given a word vector equation, predict the expected result word for a simple analogy.
Explain that vector difference can capture the relationship between two words.
Perform vector addition or subtraction to solve an analogy task.

current_subject_concepts.label: Contextualized Word Embeddings
current_subject_concepts.description: Word embeddings that are dynamic and context-dependent, produced by models such as BERT or ELMo, which use bidirectional architectures to capture word meaning in sentence context.
coverage_criteria: Explain the difference between static and contextual word embeddings.
Describe how a model like BERT or ELMo generates different embeddings for the same word in different sentences.

current_subject_concepts.label: Sparse Bag-of-Words Vectors via Dictionary and doc2bow
current_subject_concepts.description: Documents in Gensim are represented as sparse bag-of-words vectors, where each feature is a word count with zeros omitted. The Dictionary class maps words to integer IDs, and doc2bow converts tokenized documents into these vectors.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a Gensim sparse bag-of-words vector is.
Create a Dictionary from tokenized documents and use doc2bow to produce a sparse BOW vector.

current_subject_concepts.label: Building a Sequential Model with Dense Layers
current_subject_concepts.description: Construct a simple feedforward neural network using Keras Sequential model by stacking Dense layers, specifying input shape, number of units, and activation functions, and understand common activations like ReLU and softmax.
coverage_criteria: Write code to create a Sequential model with at least one Dense layer, specifying units and activation.
Explain the purpose of activation functions on hidden and output layers.
